title: Abraham de Moivre
summary: French-born Huguenot mathematician (1667-1754) who worked in London and whose Doctrine of Chances (1718; 2nd ed. 1738; 3rd ed. 1756) gave the first textbook theory of probability, stating the rules for independent and dependent events that underlie conditional probability, and who first formulated the normal approximation to the binomial in 1733.

title: Actively open-minded thinking
summary: A thinking disposition, named by Jonathan Baron, in which a person searches thoroughly and fairly for possibilities, evidence and goals, gives weight to evidence against a favoured view, and holds confidence in proportion to the search actually done.

title: Ad hominem
summary: The fallacy of rejecting a claim or argument because of some feature of the person advancing it (character, motives, circumstances or conduct) when that feature does not bear on whether the claim is true or the argument is good.
criticalQuestions: How well is the allegation about the person actually supported by evidence?
Does the person's character, interest or conduct matter in this kind of exchange, for example because we are relying on their testimony or judgment?
Would the argument still stand if someone with no stake in it had made it?
Is the attack used to lower the weight we give the speaker's say-so, or to declare the claim itself false?
Could the apparent bias or inconsistency be explained once the person is allowed to respond?

title: Affect heuristic
summary: The mental shortcut of judging risks, benefits and choices by the quick, often automatic feeling of goodness or badness a thing evokes, which makes perceived risk and perceived benefit move in opposite directions even when in reality they are independent or positively related.

title: Affirming a disjunct
summary: The invalid inference from "P or Q" and "P" to "not Q", which treats an inclusive "or" as if it ruled out both alternatives being true at once.
criticalQuestions: Could both alternatives in the "or" premise be true at the same time?
Is the "or" meant exclusively, and if so, has the "not both" claim been stated and supported?
Does the affirmed alternative by itself rule out the other one, independent of the disjunction?
What would a realistic case look like in which both options hold together?

title: Affirming the consequent
summary: The deductively invalid inference that takes a conditional "if P then Q" together with the truth of Q and concludes P, treating a sufficient condition as if it were also a necessary one.
criticalQuestions: Besides the stated antecedent, what else could make the consequent true?
Does the conditional really run both ways, or has a one-way "if" been heard as "if and only if"?
How often does the consequent occur when the antecedent is false, and has that rate been checked?
Have rival explanations of the observed consequent been compared before accepting the antecedent?

title: Alfred Tarski
summary: Polish-American logician and mathematician (1901-1983) whose 1933 definition of truth for formal languages and 1936 model-theoretic definition of logical consequence gave modern logic its standard account of what it means for an argument to be valid.

title: Ambiguity
summary: The property of a word, phrase or sentence that has more than one distinct, legitimate meaning, such as "bank" (river edge or lender) or "visiting relatives can be tiresome"; unnoticed in an argument, it lets a term or sentence shift meaning between premises and conclusion.

title: Amos Tversky
summary: Israeli-American cognitive psychologist (1937-1996) who, largely with Daniel Kahneman, showed that intuitive judgment under uncertainty relies on a few heuristics that produce systematic biases, and who co-created prospect theory.

title: Analysis of competing hypotheses
summary: A structured analytic technique, devised by the CIA analyst Richards Heuer, in which an analyst lays out every plausible explanation side by side in a matrix, scores each item of evidence against all of them, and favours the hypothesis with the least evidence against it rather than the most for it.

title: Anchoring effect
summary: The tendency for a numerical estimate or judgment to be pulled toward a previously encountered value (the anchor), even when that value is uninformative or plainly arbitrary.

title: Antilogism
summary: A single-rule test for categorical syllogisms devised by Christine Ladd(-Franklin): pair the two premises with the contradictory of the conclusion, and the syllogism is valid exactly when that trio has the shape of an inconsistent triad (two universal exclusions, one particular, with the right pattern of positive and negated terms).

title: Argument
summary: A set of statements in which one or more premises are offered as reasons in support of a further statement, the conclusion; the basic unit that logic and critical thinking evaluate.

title: Argument from analogy
summary: The presumptive argument pattern "case C1 is similar to case C2; conclusion A holds in C1; so A plausibly holds in C2". Its strength depends on whether the shared features are relevant to A, whether relevant differences undercut the comparison, and whether a rival analogy points the other way.
criticalQuestions: Are there differences between the two cases that would undermine the similarity being relied on?
Are the shared features actually relevant to the conclusion, or only superficial?
Is the conclusion really correct for the source case in the first place?
Is there another similar case where a different conclusion was reached?
Is the conclusion modest enough for the strength of the comparison?

title: Argument from expert opinion
summary: The presumptive argument pattern "E is an expert in domain S, which contains claim A; E asserts A; so A may plausibly be accepted". It is reasonable but defeasible: its strength depends on answers to critical questions about the expert's competence, field, statement, reliability, agreement with other experts and evidence.
criticalQuestions: How credible is this person as an expert, judged by training, track record and standing in the field?
Is the claim actually inside the person's field of expertise, or only next to it?
What exactly did the expert say, and does it really imply the claim being made in their name?
Is the expert personally reliable here, or do conflicts of interest or a history of bias give reason for doubt?
Do other qualified experts in the field agree, or is this a minority or disputed view?
Is the expert's statement based on evidence that could be produced and checked if asked?

title: Argument mapping
summary: A technique for laying out the inferential structure of an argument as a box-and-arrow diagram, with the main conclusion at the top and reasons, co-premises and objections beneath it, so the structure can be inspected and evaluated.

title: Argumentation schemes
summary: A framework from informal logic that catalogues the recurring patterns of everyday, defeasible argument (from expert opinion, analogy, consequences and so on) and pairs each with critical questions that test whether a particular instance holds.

title: Argumentation theory
summary: The interdisciplinary study of how people use arguments to resolve differences of opinion, combining a description of real argumentative discourse with standards of reasonableness for analysing, evaluating and producing it; it draws on logic, dialectic and rhetoric.

title: Aristotle
summary: Greek philosopher (384-322 BCE), student of Plato and founder of the Lyceum, who created the first systematic formal logic, the syllogistic, and wrote the first classification of fallacies; his logical treatises, later collected as the Organon, set the agenda for logic for two thousand years.

title: Sir Austin Bradford Hill
summary: English medical statistician and epidemiologist (1897-1991) who persuaded the UK Medical Research Council to allocate treatments by random numbers, co-designed the 1948 streptomycin trial, showed with Richard Doll that smoking is linked to lung cancer, and in 1965 set out nine viewpoints for judging whether an association is causal.

title: Availability heuristic
summary: The mental shortcut of judging how frequent or probable something is by how easily instances or associations come to mind, which works when ease of recall tracks real frequency and misleads when vividness, recency or media exposure drive recall instead.

title: Baruch Fischhoff
summary: American-Israeli decision scientist (PhD Hebrew University, 1975), Howard Heinz University Professor at Carnegie Mellon, whose 1975 experiments started research on hindsight bias and who, with Sarah Lichtenstein, helped establish overconfidence and calibration research and the study of debiasing.

title: Base-rate neglect
summary: The error of judging how likely something is from case-specific evidence alone while ignoring or underweighting how common it is in the first place (its base rate or prior probability).
criticalQuestions: Before looking at this evidence, how common is the outcome in the relevant population?
How often would this same evidence show up if the outcome were absent (the false-positive rate)?
Out of 1,000 comparable cases, how many would show the evidence and actually have the outcome?
Is the base rate I am using drawn from a reference class that really fits this case?

title: Bayesian reasoning
summary: Reasoning that treats beliefs as degrees of probability and revises them in light of evidence by Bayes' theorem: the probability of a hypothesis after the evidence combines its prior probability with how much more likely the evidence is if the hypothesis is true than if it is false.

title: Begging the question
summary: The fallacy of offering, as support for a conclusion, premises that already assume that conclusion, so the argument may be valid yet gives a doubter no independent reason to accept it.
criticalQuestions: If I set the conclusion aside, is there any reason left for believing the premises?
Would someone who doubts the conclusion already accept each premise, or only someone who agrees?
Does a key term or label in the premises quietly carry the conclusion inside it?
Traced step by step, does the chain of support loop back to the claim it is meant to prove?
Is this really an argument meant to persuade, or an explanation or definition where a loop is harmless?

title: Belief bias
summary: The tendency to judge whether an argument is logically valid by whether its conclusion is believable, so that believable conclusions are accepted from invalid arguments and unbelievable ones are rejected from valid arguments.

title: Bias blind spot
summary: The tendency to see cognitive and motivational biases more readily in other people's judgments than in one's own, so that people rate themselves as less biased than their peers.

title: Bloom's taxonomy
summary: A classification of educational objectives, first published by Benjamin Bloom and colleagues in 1956 and revised by Anderson and Krathwohl in 2001, that orders cognitive processes from remembering through understanding, applying, analyzing and evaluating to creating, and is widely used to separate "lower-order" from "higher-order" thinking in teaching and assessment.

title: Bounded rationality
summary: The idea, introduced by Herbert Simon, that real decision makers reason within limits of information, time and computational capacity, so their rationality is better described by good-enough search and stopping rules than by the global optimization of the idealised "economic man".

title: Burden of proof
summary: The obligation, carried by one side of a dispute, to support a claim with enough evidence or argument to meet the applicable standard; if the burden is not met, the claim is not accepted, though its opposite is not thereby proven.

title: Calibration
summary: The match between stated confidence and actual hit rate: a judge is well calibrated when, across many judgments given the same probability, that share of them turns out true. It is one component of probabilistic accuracy, distinct from resolution, and is measured with scoring rules such as the Brier score.

title: Categorical proposition
summary: A statement that relates two classes by saying that all, none or some of the members of a subject class are or are not included in a predicate class; its four standard forms, A, E, I and O, are the building blocks of syllogistic logic.

title: Categorical syllogism
summary: A deductive argument made of exactly three categorical propositions (two premises and a conclusion) using exactly three terms, each appearing twice; its form is fixed by its mood and figure, and validity depends on that form alone.

title: Charles Hamblin
summary: Australian philosopher and computer pioneer (1922-1985) whose book Fallacies (1970) attacked the textbook "standard treatment" of fallacies and proposed formal dialectic, rule-governed dialogue games with commitment stores, as the proper framework for studying them, helping launch modern informal logic and formal argumentation.

title: Christiaan Huygens
summary: Dutch mathematician, physicist and astronomer (1629-1695) whose Treatise on Light (written 1678, published 1690) gave an early explicit statement of the hypothetico-deductive method, holding that principles are verified by the agreement of their consequences with observation, and whose 1657 tract on games of chance introduced mathematical expectation.

title: Chrysippus
summary: Greek Stoic philosopher (c. 280-207 BCE) and third head of the Stoa, the main architect of Stoic logic, whose system of five indemonstrable arguments, starting with "if p then q; p; therefore q", made him one of the first to organise propositional logic as a discipline.

title: Cogency
summary: The property of a non-deductive argument that is inductively strong and whose premises are all actually true; in informal logic, more broadly, an argument whose premises are acceptable, relevant and sufficient for its conclusion.

title: Cognitive bias
summary: A systematic and predictable tendency for human judgment to depart from a chosen normative standard (logic, probability theory, or accurate perception), so that errors lean in a consistent direction rather than scattering at random.

title: Cognitive psychology
summary: The branch of psychology that studies mental processes such as perception, attention, memory, problem solving and reasoning, usually by running controlled experiments with people and explaining the results with models of how the mind represents and transforms information.

title: Conditional probability
summary: The probability that one event occurs given that another event occurs, standardly defined as the probability of both divided by the probability of the conditioning event (when that is above zero); the building block of Bayesian updating, independence and most statistical evidence.

title: Confirmation bias
summary: The tendency to seek out, interpret and remember evidence in ways that favour a belief or hypothesis one already holds, usually without being aware of doing so, while giving less weight to evidence that could count against it.

title: Conflict of interest
summary: A set of circumstances that creates a substantial risk that a person's professional judgment about a primary interest (a patient's welfare, the validity of research, a client's outcome) will be unduly influenced by a secondary interest such as financial gain; it names a risk of bias, not proof that bias occurred, and it is a legitimate reason to seek independent evidence.

title: Confounding
summary: The distortion of an apparent cause-and-effect relationship that occurs when the exposure and the outcome share a common cause, so that the groups being compared differ in their risk of the outcome for reasons other than the exposure itself.

title: Conjunction fallacy
summary: The error of judging a combination of two events or attributes ("A and B") to be more probable than one of them alone, which breaks the rule that a conjunction can never be more likely than either of its parts.
criticalQuestions: Is the detailed version of the claim really more likely than the shorter claim it contains?
If I strip out the extra detail, does every case that fits the detailed story still fit the short one?
Out of 100 comparable cases, how many would show A, and how many of those would also show B?
Am I rating how plausible or coherent the story sounds rather than how often it would happen?

title: Consider the opposite
summary: A debiasing technique in which a person deliberately generates reasons why their current judgment, hypothesis or reference value might be wrong, so that evidence pointing the other way becomes as available as the evidence that supports it.

title: Correcting erroneous perceptions of randomness
summary: A structured corrective technique, developed by Robert Ladouceur's group for gambling, that teaches people that random events are independent and uncontrollable, has them catch their own mistaken "due" or "I can beat it" thoughts as they occur, and corrects those thoughts on the spot.

title: Correlation versus causation
summary: The principle that a statistical association between two variables does not by itself show that one causes the other, because the pattern can also arise from a common cause, reverse causation, selection of the sample, or chance; causal conclusions need further evidence and explicit assumptions.

title: Critical thinking education
summary: The theory and practice of deliberately teaching people to reason well, covering what to teach, whether to teach it in stand-alone courses or inside subjects, and how much instruction actually improves measured reasoning and carries over to new problems.

title: Daniel Kahneman
summary: Israeli-American psychologist (1934-2024) who co-founded the heuristics-and-biases program with Amos Tversky, won the 2002 Nobel Prize in economics, and popularized the fast/slow (System 1 / System 2) account of intuition and deliberation.

title: Debiasing
summary: The family of interventions that remove or reduce systematic errors in judgment and decision making, either by changing the decision maker (education, cognitive strategies, decision models) or by changing the task and environment (incentives, accountability, choice architecture, organisational routines).

title: Debiasing training games
summary: Interactive "serious games" that teach people to recognise and reduce specific cognitive biases by having them make biased-prone judgments inside a story, then giving personalised feedback, explanation and practice; a single session has reduced biases such as the bias blind spot in laboratory tests for weeks afterwards.

title: Deductive reasoning
summary: Reasoning in which the premises are meant to guarantee the conclusion, so that if the argument is valid it is impossible for the premises to be true and the conclusion false.

title: Defeasible reasoning
summary: Reasoning whose premises give real but provisional support to a conclusion, so that the conclusion can be rationally withdrawn when new information (a defeater) arrives, even though none of the original premises is retracted.

title: Deliberate reflection
summary: A structured debiasing procedure, developed in research on medical diagnosis, in which a person who has formed a first impression lists the findings that support and contradict it, then assumes it is wrong and tests alternative explanations the same way before committing to a final judgment.

title: Delphi Report on critical thinking
aliases: Critical Thinking - A Statement of Expert Consensus for Purposes of Educational Assessment and Instruction
APA Delphi consensus on critical thinking
summary: Peter Facione's 1990 report for the American Philosophical Association, which used a six-round Delphi process with 46 experts to reach a consensus definition of critical thinking as purposeful, self-regulatory judgment, together with six core cognitive skills, a profile of critical-thinking dispositions and recommendations for instruction and assessment.

title: Denying the antecedent
summary: The deductively invalid inference that takes a conditional "if P then Q" together with the falsity of P and concludes that Q is false, overlooking every other way Q could come about.
criticalQuestions: Apart from the stated antecedent, what else could bring about the consequent?
Does the speaker actually mean "only if", and if so, has that stronger claim been stated and defended?
How likely is the consequent when the antecedent is absent, and has anyone checked?
Could the antecedent be false while the consequent still turns out true in a realistic case?

title: Devil's advocacy
summary: A structured challenge technique in which a person or subgroup is assigned to build the strongest possible case against a group's prevailing view or proposed plan, so that weak assumptions, thin evidence and overlooked alternatives surface before the decision is final.

title: Disjunctive syllogism
summary: The valid inference form "P or Q; not P; therefore Q", which reaches one alternative of a disjunction by ruling out the other.

title: Distribution of terms
summary: The traditional property of a term in a categorical proposition of being "taken universally", so that the statement says something about every member of the term's class: universals distribute their subject and negatives their predicate, and the syllogistic rules are stated in these terms.

title: Dual-process theory
summary: The family of theories holding that judgment and reasoning draw on two kinds of processing: fast, autonomous Type 1 processes that supply default answers, and slower, working-memory-dependent Type 2 processes that can reflect on, test and sometimes override those defaults.

title: Ecological rationality
summary: The view, developed by Gerd Gigerenzer, Peter Todd and the ABC Research Group, that a decision strategy is rational to the degree that it fits the information structure of the environment it is used in, so the same simple heuristic can be smart in one setting and error-prone in another.

title: Epistemology
summary: The branch of philosophy that studies knowledge and justified belief: what knowing is, what makes a belief justified, where knowledge comes from (perception, memory, reason, testimony) and how far it can reach in the face of skeptical challenges.

title: Exclusive premises
summary: The syllogistic fallacy of drawing a conclusion from two negative premises. Because each premise only excludes one class from the middle term, the premises fix no relation between the conclusion's two terms, so every categorical syllogism with two negative premises is invalid.
criticalQuestions: Are both premises negative, so that each one only says which things are excluded from the middle class?
Does anything in the premises say how the conclusion's subject and predicate relate to each other directly?
Can you describe a case where both premises are true and the conclusion is false?
Did the arguer mean a stronger affirmative claim, such as "only X can do this", that should be stated and defended?

title: Existential fallacy
summary: The formal fallacy of drawing a particular conclusion, which asserts that something exists, from universal premises that do not assert that their subject class has any members; under the modern (Boolean) reading of categorical propositions, a syllogism with two universal premises and a particular conclusion is invalid unless an existence premise is added.
criticalQuestions: Do the premises say that anything in the subject class actually exists, or only what would be true of its members?
Could the subject class be empty, as with a rule about cases that have not happened yet?
If the class is known to have members, has that existence premise been stated so the argument can be checked?
Does a Venn diagram of the premises place an X in the region the particular conclusion needs?

title: Fallacy of four terms
aliases: fallacy of more than three terms
summary: The syllogistic fallacy of an argument that looks like a categorical syllogism but uses four terms instead of three, usually because one word carries two meanings, so the middle term never actually links the subject and predicate of the conclusion.
criticalQuestions: Does each key word or phrase mean exactly the same thing in both places it appears?
If the shared term were replaced by a precise definition, would the two premises still talk about the same class?
Does the argument look valid even though its premises are true and its conclusion is plainly false?
Once the terms are counted by meaning rather than by wording, are there still only three?

title: False dilemma
summary: The fallacy of presenting too few options, usually two, as if they were the only ones available, so that rejecting one appears to force acceptance of the other.
criticalQuestions: Are the options offered really the only ones, or has a third course, a compromise or a combination been left out?
Are the options actually mutually exclusive, or could both be pursued at once?
Do the bad consequences attached to the rejected option really follow from it?
Who framed the choice, and would they benefit if the unlisted options stayed off the table?

title: Falsifiability criterion
summary: Karl Popper's proposal that a claim or theory counts as scientific only if some possible observation could show it to be false; a theory that is compatible with every conceivable outcome tells us nothing testable about the world.

title: Fast-and-frugal heuristics
summary: The research program, launched by Gerd Gigerenzer and colleagues in the mid-1990s, that models judgment as the use of simple, precisely specified rules which search little information, stop early and decide on one or a few cues, and that judges such rules by how well they fit the structure of the environment rather than by logical or statistical norms.

title: Formal fallacy
summary: An argument that is deductively invalid because of its logical structure: it instantiates an invalid form, so any argument with the same form can have true premises and a false conclusion, whatever its subject matter.

title: Formal logic
summary: The branch of logic that studies deductive inference by abstracting from what statements are about to the structures (logical forms) they share, and that states those forms in precisely defined artificial languages so that validity can be tested by form alone.

title: Framing effect
summary: The tendency for choices and evaluations to change when the same options or facts are described in logically equivalent but different ways, most often as gains versus losses or as successes versus failures.

title: Gambler's fallacy
aliases: fallacy of the maturity of chances
summary: The mistaken belief that, in a sequence of independent random events, an outcome becomes less likely after it has occurred several times in a row (or "due" after it has not), as if chance corrected itself in the short run.
criticalQuestions: Are these events actually independent, or is there a real mechanism linking one outcome to the next?
If I had walked in just now and not seen the streak, would my estimate for the next outcome be any different?
Am I expecting a short run to look like the long-run average?
Is my judgment on this case being pulled by how I decided the last few cases rather than by its own merits?

title: George Udny Yule
summary: British statistician (1871-1951) who worked with Karl Pearson, described in 1903 the reversal of associations now called Simpson's paradox, and in 1926 showed why trending time series so often produce high but meaningless "nonsense correlations".

title: Gerd Gigerenzer
summary: Psychologist and long-time Max Planck director who argued that simple, fast-and-frugal heuristics can be ecologically rational rather than error-prone, showed that natural frequencies improve Bayesian reasoning, and became the leading critic of the heuristics-and-biases program and an advocate of risk literacy.

title: Gettier problem
aliases: problem of epistemic luck in the analysis of knowledge
summary: The problem, raised by Edmund Gettier in 1963, that a person can hold a justified, true belief that still falls short of knowledge because it is true only by luck; it shows that justified true belief is not sufficient for knowing.

title: Groupthink
summary: A mode of thinking in a cohesive in-group in which members' drive for unanimity overrides realistic appraisal of alternatives, producing pressure on dissenters, self-censorship and an illusion of agreement that can lead to defective decisions; proposed by Irving Janis in 1972 and empirically contested since.

title: Hasty generalization
summary: The fallacy of drawing a general conclusion about a whole class from too few, or too unrepresentative, cases, or of treating a rule that holds only usually as if it had no exceptions.
criticalQuestions: How many cases is the conclusion based on, and is that enough for a claim this broad?
How were the cases chosen, and could the way they were found make them unusual?
Does the conclusion say "all" or "always" when the evidence supports only "many" or "usually"?
Were counterexamples looked for, and what happened to the ones that turned up?
How much is at stake if the generalization is wrong, and does that call for a higher standard of proof?

title: Heuristics and biases program
summary: The research program, launched by Amos Tversky and Daniel Kahneman around 1970, that explains intuitive judgment under uncertainty as the use of a few general-purpose heuristics (such as representativeness, availability and anchoring) which are usually serviceable but produce predictable, systematic errors when compared with normative rules.

title: Hindsight bias
summary: The tendency, once an outcome is known, to judge it as having been more predictable, more inevitable and more obvious beforehand than it actually was, and to misremember one's earlier predictions as closer to the outcome.

title: Hypothesis testing
summary: The method of evaluating a conjecture by deducing observable consequences ("test implications") from it, together with auxiliary assumptions, and then checking whether they occur: a failed prediction counts against the hypothesis, a successful one lends it support without proving it.

title: Iain Chalmers
summary: British health services researcher who, with colleagues in Oxford in the 1970s and 1980s, built the first large body of systematic reviews of randomized trials (Effective Care in Pregnancy and Childbirth, 1989), founded the UK Cochrane Centre in 1992 and co-founded the Cochrane Collaboration, and later promoted public critical thinking about treatment claims through the James Lind Initiative and the Informed Health Choices Key Concepts.

title: Ignoratio elenchi
summary: The fallacy of offering an argument, often a perfectly good one, for a conclusion other than the one actually at issue, so that it misses the point it was meant to establish or refute.
criticalQuestions: What exactly is the conclusion in dispute, stated in one sentence?
What conclusion do the premises actually support, and is it the same claim?
If the argument succeeds completely, does the disputed claim stand or fall, or is it untouched?
Does the argument contradict the opponent's thesis in the same respect, at the same time and about the same thing?
Is there a definite alternative conclusion being argued for, or is the argument simply drifting away from the issue?

title: Illicit major
aliases: illicit process of the major term
summary: The syllogistic fallacy committed when the major term (the predicate of the conclusion) is distributed in the conclusion but undistributed in the major premise, so the conclusion says something about the whole of a class that the premises described only in part.
criticalQuestions: Is the conclusion's predicate about all members of its class while the premise spoke only of some of them?
Could something outside the subject class still have the property the conclusion denies?
Does a Venn diagram of the premises leave room for the conclusion to be false?

title: Inductive reasoning
summary: Reasoning in which the premises are meant to make the conclusion probable rather than guarantee it, typically by projecting from observed cases to unobserved cases, general claims or predictions.

title: Inference to the best explanation
summary: The non-deductive inference that accepts a hypothesis because, among the available rivals, it would best explain the evidence; in its modern sense it is the standard meaning of "abduction".

title: Informal fallacy
summary: A recurring, deceptively bad pattern of argument whose flaw lies in its content, context or use (relevance, ambiguity, unwarranted assumption or dialogue misconduct) rather than in an invalid logical form that formal analysis alone could expose.

title: Informal logic
summary: The branch of logic that develops non-formal standards and procedures for identifying, interpreting, evaluating and constructing the arguments people actually make in natural language, in settings such as public debate, law, medicine, education and the workplace.

title: Information Disorder: Toward an Interdisciplinary Framework
aliases: Information Disorder: Toward an interdisciplinary framework for research and policymaking
Council of Europe information disorder report
summary: Claire Wardle and Hossein Derakhshan's 2017 report for the Council of Europe, which replaced the vague label "fake news" with a framework of three kinds of information disorder (mis-, dis- and malinformation), three elements (agent, message, interpreter) and three phases (creation, production, distribution).

title: Insensitivity to sample size
summary: The tendency to judge how likely a sample result is, or how much a sample proves, by how closely it resembles the population while ignoring how many cases it contains, so that small samples are trusted too much and their greater variability goes unnoticed.

title: Intelligence analysis
summary: The professional practice, and the body of study around it, of turning incomplete, ambiguous and sometimes deliberately deceptive information into forecasts and assessments, with stated uncertainty, that help decision makers act.

title: James Frederick Ferrier
summary: Scottish metaphysician (1808-1864), professor at St Andrews, who introduced the word "epistemology" into English in his Institutes of Metaphysic (1854) and paired it with "agnoiology", a theory of ignorance holding that we can be ignorant only of what could in principle be known.

title: John Buridan
summary: Fourteenth-century Paris arts master (c. 1300-c. 1360) and the leading logician of the later Middle Ages, who recast the syllogism as a kind of formal consequence, gave the classic rules for which terms a proposition distributes, and rejected premise pairs whose middle term is never distributed.

title: John Dewey
summary: American pragmatist philosopher and educator (1859-1952) whose book How We Think (1910) defined "reflective thinking", analysed a complete act of thought into five phases, and made the critical, inquiring habit of mind an explicit aim of schooling.

title: John Venn
summary: English logician and Cambridge don (1834-1923) who formalised the overlapping-circle diagrams that now bear his name, read universal propositions as making no claim that anything exists (so subalternation and weakened syllogisms fail), and was a founder of the frequency interpretation of probability in The Logic of Chance (1866).

title: Jonathan St B. T. Evans
summary: British cognitive psychologist at the University of Plymouth who co-introduced the idea of dual processes in reasoning with Peter Wason in 1975, proposed the heuristic-analytic theory, ran the classic belief-bias experiments and later helped redefine dual-process theory in terms of Type 1 and Type 2 processing.

title: Judgment and decision making
summary: The interdisciplinary research field, rooted in psychology, that studies how people form judgments (estimates, predictions, probabilities) and make choices, typically by comparing actual behavior with normative standards such as probability theory and expected utility and then designing ways to close the gap.

title: Justified true belief
summary: The proposal that a person knows a claim if and only if the claim is true, they believe it, and they are justified in believing it; long treated as the standard analysis of propositional knowledge until Gettier cases showed the three conditions are not jointly sufficient.

title: Karl Popper
summary: Austrian-British philosopher (1902-1994) who argued that scientific theories are bold conjectures that can never be verified but can be refuted by observation, making falsifiability the mark of science and criticism the engine of the growth of knowledge.

title: Kenneth Arrow
summary: American economist (1921-2017) whose impossibility theorem showed that no method of combining individual rankings into a group ranking can meet a short list of fairness conditions, and who, with Anthony Fisher, showed that uncertainty plus irreversibility gives a reason to keep options open.

title: Key assumptions check
summary: A structured analytic technique in which an analyst or team writes down the current line of reasoning, lists every stated and unstated premise it rests on, challenges each one, and keeps only those that must hold for the judgment to stand, together with the signs that would show they have failed.

title: Lateral reading
summary: A source-evaluation technique, borrowed from professional fact checkers, in which you leave an unfamiliar website early and search other sources about who is behind it before judging its content, instead of scrutinising the page itself.

title: Leopold von Ranke
summary: German historian (1795-1886) whose 1824 critique of earlier historians made the questions "was this writer a firsthand witness, and is this account original or borrowed?" the starting point of historical method, and whose Berlin seminar trained the first generation of professional, source-critical historians.

title: Logic
summary: The discipline that studies correct inference: which conclusions follow from which premises, why they follow, and how strongly; it includes formal (deductive) logic, inductive logic and informal logic as branches.

title: Logical necessity instructions
summary: A debiasing technique for deductive judgments in which the reasoner is told, or tells themselves, to assume the premises are true and to accept a conclusion only if it must follow from them, regardless of whether it is believable. It reduces belief bias in some studies but has not eliminated it.

title: Metacognition
summary: Knowledge about one's own cognition and the ongoing monitoring and control of it: noticing whether you understand, judging how likely an answer is to be right, and changing strategy, slowing down or seeking help in response.

title: Method of counterexample
summary: A test for invalidity: to show that an argument form does not guarantee its conclusion, describe a case or substitution instance of the same form in which every premise is true and the conclusion is false.

title: Mill's methods
summary: Five eliminative rules for identifying causes, set out by John Stuart Mill in 1843: the methods of agreement, difference, joint agreement and difference, residues, and concomitant variation, each of which rules out candidate causes by comparing cases where an effect does and does not occur.

title: Minna Cheves Wilkins
summary: Experimental psychologist whose 1928 Archives of Psychology monograph on syllogistic reasoning is the earliest study routinely cited for content and belief effects in deduction: the same logical form was handled differently depending on whether it was stated in familiar, symbolic or belief-conflicting terms.

title: Misinformation and disinformation
summary: False or misleading information in circulation: misinformation is false content shared without intent to harm, while disinformation is false content deliberately created or spread to deceive or cause harm.

title: Modus ponens
summary: The valid inference form "if P then Q; P; therefore Q", which concludes the consequent of a conditional from the conditional together with its antecedent.

title: Modus tollens
summary: The valid inference form "if P then Q; not Q; therefore not P", which concludes the denial of a conditional's antecedent from the conditional together with the denial of its consequent.

title: Natural frequency format
summary: A way of presenting or re-expressing risk information as counts of cases drawn from one concrete reference group (for example "8 of the 10 people with the condition test positive") instead of as conditional probabilities, so that the base rate stays visible and Bayesian updating becomes simple counting.

title: Necessary and sufficient conditions
summary: A necessary condition for Y is one without which Y cannot hold; a sufficient condition for Y is one whose presence guarantees Y. In a true conditional "if P then Q", P is sufficient for Q and Q is necessary for P.

title: Numeracy
summary: The ability and readiness to understand and use numbers, especially probabilities, percentages and ratios, in everyday judgment; people high in numeracy are less swayed by how information is framed and by irrelevant feelings such as mood, and respond more precisely to the numbers themselves.

title: Occam's razor
summary: The methodological principle that, other things being equal, you should prefer the explanation or theory that postulates fewer entities, causes or assumptions; it ranks rival hypotheses that fit the evidence equally well, and does not show that the simpler one is true.

title: Organon
summary: The collection of Aristotle's six logical treatises (Categories, On Interpretation, Prior Analytics, Posterior Analytics, Topics and On Sophistical Refutations), assembled and named "tool" by later Peripatetic commentators, which served as the standard textbook of logic in the Arabic and Latin traditions for some two thousand years.

title: Taking the outside view
summary: A forecasting and debiasing technique in which a person sets aside the details of the case at hand, first asks how similar cases have usually turned out, and then anchors the prediction on that distribution of outcomes before adjusting for what is special about the case.

title: Overconfidence effect
summary: The tendency for confidence in one's judgments, performance or estimates to exceed their actual accuracy, studied in three forms: overestimation of one's own performance, overplacement relative to others, and overprecision (excessive certainty that one's beliefs are correct).

title: Peter Wason
summary: British cognitive psychologist (1924-2003) at University College London whose 2-4-6 rule-discovery task and four-card selection task showed that people tend to seek confirming rather than disconfirming evidence, launching the experimental psychology of reasoning and its study of biases.

title: Philosophy of science
summary: The branch of philosophy that examines the methods, foundations and implications of science: how hypotheses are tested and confirmed, what separates science from non-science, what explanations and theories are, and how and why scientific views change.

title: Plato
summary: Athenian philosopher (c. 428/427-348/347 BCE), student of Socrates, teacher of Aristotle and founder of the Academy, whose dialogues turned Socratic question-and-answer into a written model of testing claims and, in the Theaetetus, first posed the question of whether knowledge is true belief plus an account.

title: Pope Sixtus V
summary: Franciscan pope (reigned 1585-1590) whose reorganisation of the Roman Curia created the Congregation of Rites in 1588 and is credited with establishing, in 1587, the office of Promoter of the Faith, the "devil's advocate" whose job was to argue against every candidate for sainthood.

title: Port-Royal Logic
aliases: Logic or the Art of Thinking
La Logique ou l'art de penser
summary: Antoine Arnauld and Pierre Nicole's 1662 textbook La Logique ou l'art de penser, a Cartesian reworking of traditional logic in four parts (ideas, judgment, reasoning, method) that broke with Aristotle's list of fallacies, added sophisms such as imperfect enumeration, and became the most widely read logic text from Aristotle to the end of the nineteenth century.

title: Post hoc ergo propter hoc
aliases: after this therefore because of this
summary: The fallacy of concluding that one event caused another merely because the first came before the second, treating temporal sequence alone as proof of a causal connection.
criticalQuestions: Apart from the order of events, what independent evidence links the earlier event to the later one?
Would the later event probably have happened anyway, for example through seasonal patterns, spontaneous recovery or a return from an unusual extreme?
Did anything else change at the same time that could explain the outcome?
How often does the outcome occur when the supposed cause is absent?
Is there a plausible mechanism, and has the pattern held up across repeated or controlled comparisons?

title: Posterior Analytics
summary: Aristotle's two-book treatise (4th century BCE) on demonstration and scientific knowledge, which argues that a proof yields knowledge only when its premises are true, primary and explanatory, and that the chain of proof must end in first principles grasped without demonstration.

title: Pragma-dialectics
summary: A theory of argumentation, developed by Frans van Eemeren and Rob Grootendorst at the University of Amsterdam, that models argument as an exchange of speech acts aimed at resolving a difference of opinion on the merits, and defines a fallacy as any move that breaks one of the rules of an ideal critical discussion.

title: Prebunking
summary: A pre-emptive misinformation countermeasure that warns people they may be misled and shows them, with a weakened example, the technique or false claim they are likely to meet, so that they resist it when the real attempt comes.

title: Premortem
summary: A plan-evaluation technique in which a team, before committing to a plan, imagines that it has already been carried out and has failed, then has each member independently write down the reasons it failed so those risks can be addressed in advance.

title: Primary and secondary sources
summary: The distinction between sources that give firsthand evidence from the time or place being studied (primary) and sources that report, interpret or analyse that evidence afterwards (secondary). Which label applies depends on the question being asked, not on the type of document.

title: Principle of charity
summary: The interpretive norm that, before criticising what someone has argued, you should reconstruct their claims and reasoning in the most reasonable form the text and context plausibly allow, rather than in a weaker or distorted form.

title: Prior Analytics
summary: Aristotle's two-book treatise (c. 350 BCE) that founded formal logic: it classifies two-premise deductions into three figures, proves the imperfect ones by reducing them to a handful of self-evident first-figure moods, shows invalidity by counterexample, and extends the system to necessity and possibility.

title: Problem of induction
summary: The philosophical problem, posed by David Hume, of justifying inferences from observed cases to unobserved ones: any argument that the future will resemble the past either cannot be deductive or must assume the very uniformity it is meant to prove.

title: Quantifier shift fallacy
summary: The invalid inference from "every A stands in relation R to some B" to "some single B stands in relation R to every A", which swaps the order of a universal and an existential quantifier and so turns a weak claim into a much stronger one.
criticalQuestions: Does the premise allow a different B for each A, or does it really say one B serves them all?
Can you describe a case where every A has its own B but no single B works for every A?
If the conclusion needs one B for all, what separate evidence shows that such a B exists?

title: Random sampling
summary: Choosing the members of a sample by a chance mechanism that gives every member of the population a known (often equal) chance of selection, so that the sample is likely to resemble the population and the size of its sampling error can be estimated.

title: Randomized controlled trial
summary: A comparative experiment in which participants are assigned to a treatment or a control group by a chance process, so that differences in outcomes can be attributed to the treatment rather than to how the groups were chosen.

title: Regression to the mean
summary: The statistical tendency for cases picked out because they scored unusually high or low on one measurement to score closer to the average when measured again, simply because the two measurements are imperfectly correlated. It can make chance fluctuation look like the effect of a treatment, policy or reward.

title: Representativeness heuristic
summary: The mental shortcut of judging how probable it is that a case belongs to a category, or that a sample came from a process, by how closely it resembles the category's stereotype or the process's typical output, which neglects base rates, sample size and the reliability of the evidence.

title: Researcher degrees of freedom
summary: The many often-arbitrary choices a researcher makes in framing hypotheses, designing a study, collecting and analysing data and reporting results; when those choices are made after seeing the data, or left undisclosed, they can make a false hypothesis look statistically significant.

title: Reversible and irreversible decisions
summary: The distinction between choices that can be cheaply undone once more is learned and choices that lock in their consequences; it sets how much deliberation, evidence and delay a decision deserves, and it also changes how people feel about a choice after making it.

title: Richard E. Nisbett
summary: American social psychologist at the University of Michigan whose work showed that people often cannot report the real causes of their judgments, that abstract statistical rules can be taught and transfer to everyday problems, and that habits of reasoning differ between cultures.

title: Richard Whately
summary: English logician, economist and Anglican archbishop of Dublin (1787-1863) whose Elements of Logic (1826) revived the study of logic in England and sorted fallacies into logical and material kinds, and whose Elements of Rhetoric (1828) gave argumentation theory its classic account of presumption and burden of proof.

title: Rules of the categorical syllogism
summary: A checklist test for categorical syllogisms: a standard-form syllogism is valid exactly when it satisfies a short set of rules about distribution, negative premises and quantity, and each broken rule names the formal fallacy committed, from the undistributed middle to the existential fallacy.

title: Satisficing
summary: A decision strategy, named by Herbert Simon in 1956, in which options are examined one at a time and search stops at the first option that meets a preset aspiration level, with the aspiration raised or lowered according to how easy satisfactory options prove to find.

title: Scientific method
summary: The family of practices by which the sciences build reliable knowledge of the natural world: systematic observation, experiment, inductive and deductive reasoning, model building and hypothesis testing, checked by a critical community. Philosophers now mostly doubt that a single fixed recipe captures it.

title: Sherman Kent
summary: American historian and intelligence officer (1903-1986) who moved from Yale to wartime research and analysis and then led the CIA's national estimates office, wrote the 1949 book that set out the methods of strategic intelligence, and pressed analysts to state their uncertainty in calibrated words of estimative probability.

title: SIFT
summary: A four-step routine for checking online claims and sources quickly: Stop, Investigate the source, Find better coverage, and Trace claims, quotes and media to their original context. It replaces close inspection of a page with brief checks of what the rest of the web says about it.

title: Simpson's paradox
summary: A statistical pattern in which an association between two variables that holds in a whole population weakens, vanishes or reverses direction once the population is split into subgroups, so that pooled and stratified data point to opposite conclusions.

title: Slippery slope
summary: An argument that a proposed first step should be rejected because it would set off a chain of further steps ending in an unacceptable outcome; it is fallacious when the chain, the point of no return or the outcome's likelihood is asserted rather than supported.
criticalQuestions: What are the intermediate steps between the first move and the feared outcome, and is each one supported by evidence rather than just asserted?
Why would we lose the ability to stop partway, and could a clear rule or bright line be drawn to halt the slide?
How likely is the final outcome, and is it really as bad as claimed?
Is the argument just a warning about bad consequences dressed up as an unstoppable chain?

title: Socratic method
summary: A method of inquiry by disciplined question and answer, modelled on Socrates in Plato's dialogues, in which a person's stated belief is examined against their other commitments until inconsistencies, hidden assumptions or gaps in their reasons come to light; used today in teaching, law schools and cognitive therapy.

title: Sophistical Refutations
summary: Aristotle's short treatise (4th century BCE), the last work of the Organon and a closing section of the Topics, on arguments that only appear to refute a thesis; its list of thirteen fallacies, six dependent on language and seven not, is the first systematic theory of fallacies and the root of the traditional fallacy lists still taught today.

title: Soundness
summary: The property of a deductive argument that is valid and whose premises are all actually true; a sound argument therefore guarantees a true conclusion.

title: Source credibility
summary: The degree to which the origin of a claim (a person, outlet or document) is perceived as competent and willing to tell the truth on the matter at hand, usually analysed as expertise plus trustworthiness; it legitimately bears on how far to rely on testimony, and it measurably shifts how persuasive a message is.

title: Square of opposition
summary: A diagram that arranges the four categorical statement forms (A, E, I, O) at the corners of a square and labels the logical relations between them: contradictories, contraries, subcontraries and subalterns, which together license immediate inferences from the truth or falsity of one statement to the others.

title: Stasis theory
summary: A classical rhetorical framework for locating the exact point at issue in a dispute by asking, in order, whether the disagreement is about fact, definition, quality or policy, so that arguments address the question that actually divides the parties.

title: Statistical reasoning training
summary: A debiasing technique that teaches abstract statistical and probability rules, such as the law of large numbers and the rule that a conjunction can be no more likely than its parts, with worked examples, so that people apply them to everyday judgments. Short training reduces errors such as the conjunction fallacy and sample-size neglect, but rarely eliminates them.

title: Stephen Toulmin
summary: British-born philosopher (1922-2009) whose book The Uses of Argument (1958) challenged the idea that good reasoning must take the form of formal deduction and gave argumentation theory its claim-data-warrant layout.

title: Stoic logic
summary: The logic developed by the Stoic school of ancient Greece, above all by Chrysippus (3rd century BCE): a system of whole propositions joined by connectives such as "if", "or", "and" and "not", with five basic argument forms (the indemonstrables) and rules for reducing other arguments to them; it is the earliest substantial forerunner of modern propositional logic.

title: Straw man fallacy
summary: The fallacy of replacing an opponent's actual position with a distorted, weaker or invented version, refuting that substitute, and presenting the refutation as if it defeated the real position.
criticalQuestions: Would the other side recognise this description as their own position, stated in their own terms?
Is the view being refuted what was actually said, or an exaggerated, absolute or invented version of it?
If the weakest argument has been answered, have the stronger arguments for the same conclusion been addressed too?
Who exactly holds the position being attacked, or is it attributed only to a vague "some people"?
Does refuting this version leave the original claim standing?

title: Structured analytic techniques
summary: A family of step-by-step procedures, developed mainly in US intelligence analysis, that externalise an analyst's reasoning (listing assumptions, laying evidence against rival hypotheses, arguing the other side, imagining alternative futures) so that mind-sets can be exposed and challenged; widely taught, but with thin and mixed evidence that they improve accuracy.

title: Sunk cost fallacy
summary: The tendency to keep investing in, or keep using, something because of money, time or effort already spent and unrecoverable, even though only future costs and benefits should bear on the decision.

title: Suppressed evidence
summary: The fallacy of presenting only the evidence that favours a conclusion while leaving out information one knows or suspects is relevant and significant, especially information that would weaken it.
criticalQuestions: What evidence on this question exists that the arguer has not mentioned, and would it point the other way?
How were the cited cases, studies or figures chosen, and could the selection itself explain the result?
Does the arguer have a stake that gives them a reason to leave out unfavourable facts?
If the full record were laid out, including the misses, would the conclusion still look as strong?
Is the omitted material actually relevant and significant, or just detail that does not bear on the conclusion?

title: Syllogism
summary: A deductive argument with two premises and a conclusion in which the premises share a linking element (in the categorical case, a middle term) that drops out of the conclusion; the family includes categorical, hypothetical and disjunctive syllogisms.

title: Systematic review
summary: A review of research that answers a clearly formulated question by finding, selecting, appraising and synthesising all eligible studies with explicit methods fixed in advance, so that the choice of evidence cannot be bent toward a preferred answer.

title: The New Rhetoric
aliases: The New Rhetoric - A Treatise on Argumentation
summary: Chaïm Perelman and Lucie Olbrechts-Tyteca's 1958 treatise on argumentation (English translation 1969), which recasts argument as an effort to win an audience's adherence rather than to prove truths, and which catalogues the starting points and argument schemes used in practical and value-laden reasoning; it is one of the founding works of modern argumentation theory.

title: Topics
summary: Aristotle's eight-book treatise (4th century BCE) on dialectic, the question-and-answer practice of attacking and defending a thesis from generally accepted opinions, which gives the earliest surviving systematic account of how arguments are found, built and tested, and whose catalogue of argument strategies (topoi) is the ancestor of modern argumentation schemes.

title: Toulmin model of argument
summary: Stephen Toulmin's six-part layout for analysing practical arguments: a claim supported by data, licensed by a warrant that rests on backing, tempered by a qualifier and open to rebuttal.

title: A Tradecraft Primer
aliases: A Tradecraft Primer: Structured Analytic Techniques for Improving Intelligence Analysis
summary: The US Government's short 2009 handbook of structured analytic techniques for intelligence analysts, which explains how mind-sets and cognitive biases distort judgment and sorts twelve techniques into diagnostic, contrarian and imaginative groups, including the key assumptions check.

title: Truth table
summary: A mechanical test for arguments in propositional logic: list every combination of truth values for the simple sentences, compute each premise and the conclusion on every row, and the argument is valid exactly when no row makes all the premises true and the conclusion false.

title: Tu quoque
summary: The fallacy of rejecting a claim, advice or criticism on the grounds that the person making it does not act in line with it, as if the speaker's inconsistency showed the claim itself to be false.
criticalQuestions: Does the speaker's conduct actually bear on whether the claim is true, or only on the speaker's character?
Are the speaker's situation and the situation the advice addresses really alike, or is the "inconsistency" a false double standard?
Is the lapse a settled habit, or a one-off failure, a past choice, or a matter of weak will that the speaker admits?
Is the claim resting on the speaker's own authority, or is it supported by independent evidence that the charge leaves untouched?
Does the speaker's failure to follow the advice suggest the advice is impractical, and if so, is that the point being made?

title: Undistributed middle
summary: The syllogistic fallacy committed when the middle term, the term shared by both premises, is not distributed in either premise, so each premise may be about a different part of its class and nothing links the conclusion's two terms.
criticalQuestions: Is the shared term ever used to speak about every member of its class, in either premise?
Could the two groups in the conclusion each overlap a different part of the shared class?
Would I still accept this form if the conclusion were something I believed to be false?

title: Validity
summary: The property of a deductive argument whose form makes it impossible for all the premises to be true and the conclusion false; validity concerns the link between premises and conclusion, not whether the premises are actually true.

title: Value-focused thinking
summary: A decision technique developed by decision analyst Ralph Keeney in which the decision maker first states what they fundamentally care about as explicit objectives, then uses those objectives to create and judge alternatives, instead of starting from whatever options happen to be on the table.

title: Venn diagram test
summary: A visual decision procedure for categorical syllogisms: draw three overlapping circles for the three terms, record only what the premises say (shading for empty regions, an X for "at least one"), and the argument is valid exactly when the conclusion can be read off the finished diagram.

title: William J. McGuire
summary: American social psychologist (1925-2007), long at Yale, who in the early 1960s proposed inoculation theory: beliefs can be made resistant to persuasion by exposing people to weakened attacks and refuting them in advance, the idea behind today's prebunking of misinformation.

title: William Whewell
summary: English philosopher, historian of science and Master of Trinity College, Cambridge (1794-1866), who built a theory of scientific induction from the history of the sciences, proposed prediction of new phenomena and the "consilience of inductions" as tests of a theory, debated John Stuart Mill on induction, and coined the word "scientist".
